entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Andouin Aubert, a prominent French jurist and ecclesiastic, rose through the ranks of the Avignon Papacy during the mid-14th century, ultimately serving as a Cardinal. Born into a noble family in Limousin, he was a nephew of Pope Innocent VI, a relationship that significantly propelled his career at a time when the papacy was deeply embroiled in European political and ecclesiastical struggles, particularly the Hundred Years' War and the nascent tensions leading to the Western Schism. His influence stemmed from his legal acumen and his strategic positioning within the powerful papal curia, making him a key figure in the administrative machinery of the Church.

Aubert began his career as a professor of civil law at the University of Toulouse, where his legal expertise was recognized. He quickly ascended through the church hierarchy, becoming Bishop of Maguelone in 1352 and then Archbishop of Embrun in 1353. His elevation to Cardinal-priest of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in December 1353 by his uncle, Pope Innocent VI, solidified his standing. As a cardinal, he played an active role in the papal administration, participating in the consistories and advising on crucial matters of canon law, diplomacy, and finance for the Avignon Popes, particularly during the turbulent pontificate of Innocent VI, until his death on May 18, 1363.

Aubert's career exemplifies the nepotism and political maneuvering characteristic of the Avignon Papacy, yet he also contributed to the legal and administrative strength of the curia. His work helped to consolidate papal authority in a period of intense challenge from secular rulers and internal church dissent, including the ongoing efforts to restore papal control over the Papal States. He was involved in the financial management of the church, including the collection of revenues that supported both papal court expenses and military efforts in Italy, crucial for maintaining the papacy's temporal power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andouin Aubert was a significant figure within the Avignon Papacy, demonstrating how legal expertise and familial ties shaped high ecclesiastical office and contributed to papal governance during a period of intense political and religious upheaval. His career exemplifies the administrative and legal efforts to consolidate papal power amidst the Hundred Years' War.
